title: SQL Examples
description: Copy-ready SQL snippets for everyday tasks: filtering and sorting, pattern search, inserting and updating, creating tables, joins, grouped reports, subqueries, date grouping, views and transactions. Every example runs against the sample shop database.

examples.title: Filter and sort products
examples.description: Select three columns, keep the rows under a price limit and sort them, the shape of most everyday queries.
examples.code:
SELECT name, category, price
FROM products
WHERE price < 20
ORDER BY price;
examples.output:
name         | category    | price
-------------+-------------+------
Sticky notes | Stationery  | 2.75
Notebook     | Stationery  | 4.5
Mouse pad    | Office      | 8.99
USB cable    | Electronics | 12

examples.title: Search with LIKE and IN
examples.description: Find customers whose name contains a letter and who live in one of several countries, combining a pattern with a list.
examples.code:
SELECT name, country
FROM customers
WHERE name LIKE '%a%' AND country IN ('UK', 'US')
ORDER BY name;
examples.output:
name              | country
------------------+--------
Ada Lovelace      | UK
Grace Hopper      | US
Margaret Hamilton | US

examples.title: Insert several rows and get their ids
examples.description: A multi-row INSERT with RETURNING, which hands back the generated ids without a second query (SQLite 3.35+, PostgreSQL, MariaDB).
examples.code:
INSERT INTO products (name, category, price) VALUES
  ('Desk lamp', 'Office', 24.90),
  ('Pen set', 'Stationery', 6.25)
RETURNING id, name, price;

examples.title: Order details across three tables
examples.description: Join orders to customers and products and compute a rounded line total, the query behind almost every invoice or order screen.
examples.code:
SELECT o.id, c.name AS customer, p.name AS product, o.quantity,
       ROUND(p.price * o.quantity, 2) AS line_total
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
JOIN products p ON p.id = o.product_id
ORDER BY o.id;
examples.output:

examples.title: Revenue per category
examples.description: A grouped report with two aggregates, a HAVING filter on the total and a sort by the computed revenue.
examples.code:
SELECT p.category,
       SUM(o.quantity) AS items,
       ROUND(SUM(p.price * o.quantity), 2) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN products p ON p.id = o.product_id
GROUP BY p.category
HAVING SUM(p.price * o.quantity) > 30
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
examples.output:
category    | items | revenue
------------+-------+--------
Electronics | 4     | 202
Office      | 3     | 57.48
Stationery  | 14    | 45.5

examples.title: Products above the average price
examples.description: A scalar subquery computes the average once; the outer query compares every product against it.
examples.code:
SELECT name, price
FROM products
WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products)
ORDER BY price DESC;
examples.output:
name                | price
--------------------+------
Mechanical keyboard | 89
Monitor stand       | 39.5

examples.title: Orders per month
examples.description: Group by a formatted date to produce a monthly summary; strftime extracts the year and month from ISO dates.
examples.code:
SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', ordered_on) AS month,
       COUNT(*) AS orders,
       SUM(quantity) AS items
FROM orders
GROUP BY month
ORDER BY month;

examples.title: A reusable report view
examples.description: Wrap a three-table aggregate in a view so the spending report becomes a one-line SELECT for everyone.
examples.code:
CREATE VIEW customer_totals AS
SELECT c.name, c.country, ROUND(SUM(p.price * o.quantity), 2) AS spent
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
JOIN products p ON p.id = o.product_id
GROUP BY c.id;
SELECT * FROM customer_totals ORDER BY spent DESC;
examples.output:
OK: CREATE VIEW customer_totals AS

name              | country     | spent
------------------+-------------+------
Ada Lovelace      | UK          | 102.5
Guido van Rossum  | Netherlands | 89
Linus Torvalds    | Finland     | 57.48
Grace Hopper      | US          | 28.5
Margaret Hamilton | US          | 27.5

examples.title: Money transfer in a transaction
examples.description: Two updates wrapped in BEGIN and COMMIT so the transfer is applied completely or not at all; a CHECK constraint guards against overdrafts.
examples.output:

OK: INSERT INTO accounts (owner, balance) VALUES ('Ada', 100), ('Grace', 50)
OK: BEGIN
OK: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 25 WHERE owner = 'Ada'
OK: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 25 WHERE owner = 'Grace'
OK: COMMIT

owner | balance
------+--------
Ada   | 75
Grace | 75
